summary: Questions about what the alphabet sum promises
lead: Try the small example before opening an answer. These questions concern its conditions, not a secure way to send a message.

rows.title: Do twenty-six possibilities mean twenty-six equal chances?
rows.question: Open the candidate table and choose Zero half the time, other numbers equally. Count the possible originals, then compare their chances.
rows.answer: All twenty-six originals remain possible. With the supplied equal prior for originals and independent biased keys, the ciphertext letter itself has chance fifty percent; each other original has chance two percent. Possibility is not equal probability. Different prior assumptions could give different chances.

rows.title: Does cancelling the reused key reveal both letters?
rows.question: Open the deliberate reuse example. Change only its key and compare the two modular differences.
rows.answer: The ciphertext difference stays equal to the message difference because the same key cancels. That relation alone does not identify both original letters. It is information that the separate one-use example did not promise to reveal; another known original would make it more damaging.

rows.title: Does secrecy tell you who sent a letter?
rows.question: Change the ciphertext by one and subtract the same key. Does the instrument reject the altered letter?
rows.answer: No. Adding one to the ciphertext adds one modulo twenty-six to the recovered original. The bare sum has no sender check. The one-time secrecy conditions do not, by themselves, authenticate a message; real messaging needs a separate authenticated construction.
